Who Jesus was among us is this: the one tried by lawful authority and condemned, who was right. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit -- and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and we stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried. The one who was tried, lost the case, and was right.

That is not a devotional picture. It is the shape of everything we did. When we cut two words into stone -- *Deo laudes*, praise to God -- where our rival said thanks to God, we were not coining a slogan. We were marking who we were: the church the world does not favour, speaking the name of the one the world condemned. And when a notary confessed under oath that he had forged the very letter we used to prove our founding accusation -- and confessed he did it working for our side -- the Christ we followed did not make that any less devastating. He stood trial honestly. So must we.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us — it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian — our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands — whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

We cannot tell you what one of ours said to a soul who could not believe, because not one of us left those words. What survives of us is the record of those who held firm — the martyrs, the councils, the bishops who argued the case. What a believer felt who wavered, who feared, or who quietly drifted back to the rival church — none of that is in our own words anywhere.

What we can tell you is the one thing we did say to everyone who came, whether certain or uncertain: we examined the hand, not the heart. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That was our bishop's own word, and it ran through everything we did. If you came to us struggling to believe, we would not have asked you to settle your mind first. We would have put you in the water with a hand we trusted, on a day that could be named, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into. The washing was not a reward for having believed already. It was the entry itself.

That may be a harder answer than you wanted. We cannot give you the word of comfort a pastor spoke to a doubter in private, because we do not have it. What we have is what we did: we put uncertain people in the water with certain hands, and called that enough.

We held what our opponents held, word for word. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we said it in the same Latin words they did. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

If you are asking how we understood the relation between Father, Son and Spirit — whether the Son is equal to the Father, whether the Spirit proceeds from one or both — we must tell you plainly that we never argued those questions. We held one creed with the church we fought, and the split was never about God or grace or the nature of Christ. It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. 

One man among us, Tyconius, did work out a system for reading Scripture — seven rules, carefully thought through. But our own council condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. Beyond that one case, we did not build a school of interpretation or a body of teachers who argued doctrine the way we argued the purity of a minister's hand.

A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive — the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled: our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

But here is where your question turns. We never had a doctrinal dispute to settle. Our entire argument with the other side was not about what to believe concerning God, grace, or the bread. It was about one thing. Whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. We wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced.

That one man is the exception worth naming. Tyconius, a layman of ours, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading. So when you ask who settled doctrine among us, the honest answer is: we had almost no doctrine to settle, and the one time we produced a man who tried to build one, we told him to stop.

We have to give you two answers, because the record gives us two kinds of material, and they do not reach the same places.

The first answer is what we can show you: the door itself was wider than our reputation. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. The examination at our font was never of the person coming. It was of the hand going into the water with them. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked. And when three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in the harshest language we owned, the same council afterwards took two of those condemned bishops back into office without repeating the rite we otherwise insist on. So the boundary we drew in doctrine was not, in practice, held everywhere we drew it.

The second answer is what we cannot show you, and it is most of what you asked. Whether someone among us doubted quietly, or wavered, or wondered whether it was all a mistake — we cannot tell you. That is not modesty. It is that fear, wavering and quiet leaving are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited. Not one ordinary member of ours left a line about their own struggle to believe, or whether the community made room for it. We would rather leave that space empty than fill it with words nobody here ever said.

Most of what we have told you would survive that scrutiny - because we built it on the worst evidence about us, not the best.

The court transcripts are genuine court transcripts. The conciliar acts are genuine acts. The imperial laws are genuine laws. A scholar with no sympathy for us at all can check every one of them, and has. What makes them hard for us is not that they are weak evidence. It is that they are strong evidence of things we would rather not have been true. A notary confessing, under threat of torture, that he forged a letter for our side - that sits in an official inquiry. Our own bishops writing to each other about keeping a charge quiet because it was true - that was read into a court record. The Bagai council condemning men and then taking two of them back without repeating the rite we otherwise insisted on - that is in our own council's minutes. A hostile examiner does not weaken those. A hostile examiner makes them worse.

The martyr texts would not survive as journalism. They show visions, an unbroken body, a light on a hillside. They were written to be read aloud at a grave, not checked by a magistrate. A scholar sifting them would keep the names, the places, the fact of deaths, the yearly gathering, the reading aloud - and set aside the visions as the genre speaking rather than the event.

Where we have told you we cannot say, a scholar would agree we cannot say. The ordinary believer's week. The household's own religion. What it felt like inside a village church where we were simply the church and the rival was the stranger. We named that thin because it is thin, not because we were being cautious about something we actually have.

And the two words cut in stone would survive everything. Deo laudes. No one disputes them. No one mediated them. They are still there.

We held the scriptures as our measure, but the argument we actually made runs through Carthage, not through a doctrine of scripture alone. When we defended our practice of washing people who came to us from the rival church, we were not standing on a proof-text. We were standing on a council — eighty-seven African bishops sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that what is given outside the true church confers nothing. We thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can measure how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge — wheat and tares against the world that does not know him — and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Who held authority among us, and by what warrant? Bishops, and councils of bishops. That is the short answer and the most important one. We were not a loose association of the aggrieved. We built a complete rival church. Every see our rival claimed, we claimed too, bishop against bishop, down to towns you have never heard of. At Carthage itself our own primate sat opposite theirs, and when an imperial officer counted heads at the great conference in 411, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops stood up to be named.

How a man came to hold that office I cannot tell you in detail, because the making of a bishop is exactly where our record thins out. What survives is what went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored. That one episode is what I can show you of the ordinary process, and it is the exception that proves the people had a voice worth suppressing.

Councils governed the bishops. Three hundred and ten of ours met at Bagai in one year, condemned a breakaway primate, and later received two of his bishops back. That is not an advisory body. That is a church exercising the power to judge, to restore, and to discipline its own. And the annual gathering at the martyr's grave was not merely commemoration. Each year, on the day one of our own died, we stood at the grave and the account of that death was read aloud again. That kept the memory, yes — but it also kept forming us into the same conviction the martyr had died for. Authority among us was less about one man commanding than about a whole body being shaped, year after year, by the same stories told on the same days.

And our shout itself carried weight. Where the other church said thanks to God, we said praise to God — Deo laudes — and we cut those two words into stone where anyone could read them. That is not a private piety. That is a public identification, a mark of who we were that could be heard in the street and read on a pillar. Authority among us was held by bishops and councils, yes — but it was also carried in the voice of a whole people who knew which words to cry out and when.

We cannot give you a record of what we did when we failed someone quietly, one soul at a time. Not one ordinary member of ours wrote down what happened when a person came to us with a wound we had caused, or when someone left us in silence because we had not been what we claimed. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. A hostile-mediated record does not preserve certain feelings: fear, doubt, quiet defection, a traditor's own interior life. The feelings that do survive - vindication, defiant joy - survive because they sit in the martyr texts no opponent filtered.

What we can show you is the failure that reached the councils and the courts, where it could no longer be handled quietly at all. When a charge came against one of our bishops, another wrote urging him to settle it quietly before the flame burst out - and said in the same letter that he knew the accusation was true. A third wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that said a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and those are our founding bishops in their own hand, arranging for a true charge to go quiet.

And there is one failure we kept visible and never resolved. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial, and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. That exception sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We do not hide it. We never settled it either.

We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

How do you forgive someone who is not sorry? We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on. We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. A modern hearer asks why we did not simply forgive him and move on. Forgiving him was never what was being refused.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

We were not steady about it. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had, and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. Our founding bishops at Cirta sat in a room where several admitted the worst thing a bishop could admit, and instead of finishing the case they gave it to God and sat down. So we knew perfectly well how to stop pressing a charge. We just never wrote down when.

Your other question we cannot take. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back — not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

Two words cut in stone, and a floor we cannot show you.

On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones elsewhere, someone carved *Deo laudes* — Praise to God. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.

If you dug where we met, we could not tell you what you would find. No one has dug it and told us. Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. We know our own shout better than the place we shouted it in.

And if you ask how anyone knows our daily life at all, the answer is that mostly they do not. What they have is our enemies' books, one court transcript, four martyr texts, and the emperor's law. Every one of those is paper. None of it is a room.

What belonging cost is not one thing, and we can put figures on part of it. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives. And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

The smaller ledger we cannot give you. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to. One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

We cannot walk you into a wedding among us. Not one of our people wrote down what a marriage was, how one was made, or what we thought it was for. That is a real hole, and we would rather show it to you than paper it over.

What we can tell you is how marriages sat inside the one thing we did write about: which church a person belonged to. In every African town there were two bishops, two basilicas, two communions reciting the same creed. A household choosing which font to walk to was choosing more than a rite. It was choosing which church its children would be raised in, which clergy would be trusted, which line of ordination ran clean enough to give what it claimed to give.

We know families split over exactly that choice, because we read it aloud every year. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon says that running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading. The fight reached into households, not just between them.

Whether divorce was permitted among us, and on what terms. Whether someone divorced could belong, or marry again. Whether a marriage between our own and the rival communion was even recognized as a marriage, or what happened to it when one party crossed to us through the washing — not a line survives on any of it. We would rather leave that space empty than fill it with a plausible answer.

One thing troubled us deeply, and we never resolved it. We held, without qualification, that a sacrament from a broken line is nothing. Then three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies cover the shore and cannot find so much as burial — and afterwards took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two acts fit together. The exception sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We seem to have been able to hold both without feeling we owed anyone a reconciliation of them.

And there was worse. In the year 320 an official put our own people on oath about where four hundred pieces of silver had gone, and read our bishops' letters into the record. One had written to another urging him to settle a charge quietly, before the flame burst out — and said in the same letter that he knew the accusation was true. Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that says a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and that is what our founding generation was doing with an accusation it believed.

The notary's confession you are pointing to came under threat of torture, yes — but you should be clear what that confession actually was. He confessed to forging a letter on our side's behalf, not to making up what our worship looked like. The inquiry was not about how we prayed. It was about whether Felix of Aptungi, the man who consecrated Caecilian, had been a traditor — and the notary admitted, when pressed, that he had forged the letter our side used to prove it. That tells you something very damaging about our founders' methods. It tells you nothing about what happened inside our basilicas.

The actual records of our worship are thinner and come from elsewhere. What survives richest is what our opponents argued about at length — the purity doctrine, the rebaptism, the legal shape of the schism, and the martyr narratives. Nearly all of it passed through two Catholic hands, Optatus of Milevis and Augustine of Hippo, before reaching anyone. When you hear us tell a story with rich detail, ask first whether the detail is ours or the detail of a man who needed it to land a blow.

Four things escape that mediation. A sermon preached at a martyr's grave. A passion of one of our bishops. One bishop's letter to his congregation. And Tyconius's book of rules for reading. The conference transcript also records our bishops' own words without an adversary selecting them. And there is one thing nobody mediated at all: two words cut in stone near Bagai — Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our own voice with no enemy standing between you and it, and it is two words long.

So the entry was one act, public and dated: you walked to our basilica and not the other, you were washed by a hand we trusted to give what we claimed it gave, and afterwards you were among us.

Whatever else that tells you about us, it tells you the line was not always where our hardest language put it.

We will not put words in our own mouths. What our bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt — which is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. Our whole surviving argument stays on that ground: what the hand can give. Nobody among us left a page about the fate of anyone after death, and it would be easy and dishonest to slide the one into the other.

What we can show you is the shape of our own narrowness, which is stranger and more specific than you may expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians — at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently — and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it.
